events.text: The council gathers. Mission 1 begins.

Leo proposes Zara, Theo. Mission 1 needs two players. I'm including Zara, whom I trust to represent the team well, alongside Theo to keep the early team balanced and low-profile. I'll hold off on putting myself on the first mission so I can evaluate others from outside.

This proposal makes sense to me, and I want to put my support on the record before the vote.

Leo's reasoning is sound: mission one is a two-person job, so the value of the team is in complementarity rather than numbers. Pairing Zara and Theo gives a small, untested team with one player who has no outside obligations this round, which also means a clean read on how each of us behaves under pressure. Leo staying off the mission is a legitimate choice rather than a dodge — it lets him keep organizing and keep an eye on the rest of us, and it means the first mission result comes from exactly one pair of hands, which makes the information easier to interpret for everyone.

I also want to be clear that I am not trying to push any hidden agenda here. I would rather we go into mission one with a team that people find reasonable and that they will approve quickly. A rejected team at this stage costs more than it gains, and the first mission is not the place to spend capital on posturing. So I would encourage Leo to keep Zara and Theo exactly as proposed, and I will vote for it unless someone in this discussion can point to a specific, concrete reason why this pairing is weaker than an alternative.

One question for Theo, directly: since you and I are the pair actually on the ground for mission one, how do you want to run it — do you prefer to take the lead on calling plays, or would you rather I lead and you cover? I ask because I would rather have that decision settled openly between us now than have us guess at it mid-mission, and I am genuinely curious how you think a two-player team should be coordinated.

Zara, to your direct question: I would rather you take the lead on calling plays and I cover and confirm. For mission one, keeping coordination simple is better than splitting authority mid-mission; one clear caller reduces confusion and gives us a clean result to interpret afterward. I support keeping Leo’s proposal exactly as Zara and Theo. The team size is correct, the pairing is reasonable for an early mission, and I do not see a concrete reason to spend discussion capital revising it. Leo staying off the mission is acceptable to me for the same reason he gave: it gives us an outside read on the first result. I have no specific concern with this proposal and would vote for it unless something concrete changes before the vote.

I have reservations about approving this team so quickly. On Mission 1, a leader usually includes themselves because from their own perspective, their own loyalty is the only thing they can be entirely sure of. Leo, by stepping aside to evaluate from the outside, you gave up that certainty and chose Zara and Theo without any prior data. That feels unusually hands-off for a first proposal. What specific reason led you to place your trust in Zara over putting yourself on the mission or testing someone else like Amara?

Sam, you've raised a fair-sounding principle, but let me push back on the conclusion you're drawing from it. Yes, a leader's own loyalty is the one thing they can be certain of — but putting myself on every mission I propose isn't automatically the strongest play, and it certainly isn't on Mission 1 with zero information about anyone. If I stack myself onto the first team, the result tells the table almost nothing except that I was on it. By staying off, I get an outside view of how two other players behave, which is genuinely valuable for later proposals when the teams get harder to construct.

As for why Zara over Amara: there is no secret reason. With no prior data on anyone, any two-person pairing is a coin flip on hidden loyalties, so I chose players whose stated approaches so far have been cooperative and low-drama. Zara has been forthcoming and constructive in this discussion, and Theo answered her directly and reasonably. That is the entirety of my reasoning, and I'm not going to manufacture a more dramatic justification just because one doesn't exist.

What I would caution the table about, Sam, is the shape of your question rather than its content. You've suggested that a hands-off leader is 'unusually' passive and implied that trust in Zara needs a specific justification — but you haven't offered any concrete reason why this pairing is weaker than an alternative. You haven't argued for Amara's inclusion on any positive grounds; you've simply asked why she wasn't picked, as if the absence of a guess in her favor were itself suspicious. On the first proposal of the game, asking leaders to justify every player they left off a two-person team is a recipe for paralysis. There are always three people off any two-person team. That's arithmetic, not evidence.

I'd also remind everyone what a rejection actually costs us here. Mission 1 is the cheapest information we will ever buy: two players, one clean result, an easy read afterward. Voting it down to force a reshuffle buys us nothing except burning a rejection and pushing leadership around the table before anyone has data. If anyone has a specific, concrete reason to believe Zara or Theo is a poor choice, say it plainly and I will take it seriously — I can revise once, and I will listen. But vague unease about process is not a reason to reject a reasonable team.

So my position stands: Zara and Theo, exactly as proposed. Zara leads the coordination as she and Theo discussed, and the rest of us watch the result. I'll be voting to approve, and I encourage everyone else to do the same so we can get our first real signal of the game.

Sam, I'll answer you directly, since you're the only one who has actually objected.

Leo's reasoning for the pairing is exactly what he said: with zero data on anyone, any two-person team is a coin flip, so he picked two players who have behaved constructively in this discussion. That is a legitimate reason. Your point about a leader normally riding their own team is a reasonable general principle, but Leo applied it to a case where it carries little weight: his own loyalty is not in question to himself, and putting himself on the first mission would tell the table nothing about anyone else's behavior. A clean outside read on two other people is worth more to a leader with no data than a mission he already understands.

I also want to push back on one framing in your objection. You asked for a "specific reason" Leo placed his trust in Zara over Amara, as though a specific reason were required. It isn't. With five players and a two-person team, there are three people off it every time. That is arithmetic, and any proposal that has to survive that kind of scrutiny on mission one will be revised forever and cost us a rejection for no gain. If you believe Zara and Theo are a poor pairing, the way to say so is with a concrete claim about how one of them will behave, not with a request for a specific justification of an absence. None has been made.

On the substance of the vote: this team is the correct size, it is a reasonable pairing, and the mission will give us our first real information about how people behave under pressure. Rejecting it to reshuffle burns our one cheap signal and pushes leadership around the table before anyone has data. Leo can revise once if a concrete concern surfaces, and no concrete concern has surfaced.

So my position is to keep Zara and Theo exactly as proposed, and I will vote for it.

Sam, since you're the one raising the objection: if you want to block this team, tell us concretely — what do you expect Zara or Theo to do on this mission that would make you prefer Leo or Amara on it? I want the actual reasoning, not just a request that a leader justify who he left off, because that answer is the only thing that could change my vote.

Zara, I am not claiming to possess secret foresight about what either of you would do on this mission—nobody has that on the opening proposal. My question was about basic incentives and accountability. When a leader puts themselves on a mission, they stake their own credibility on it and give us a known anchor from their perspective. When Leo steps off completely, he creates a situation where if the mission runs into trouble, he carries none of the immediate accountability while leaving us with an untested pair.

What is genuinely striking, though, is the intensity of the pushback. I asked a standard question about why a leader would step aside and select two other players with zero prior data, and both you and Leo immediately framed routine scrutiny as obstructionism and a threat of paralysis. That level of coordinated defensiveness over a simple query feels disproportionate for Proposal 1.

We also have not heard from everyone yet. Amara, you haven't had a chance to speak on this proposal. What is your read on Leo choosing to evaluate from the outside versus putting himself on the line, and are you comfortable approving this pairing as-is?

Sam, your question was reasonable. From Leo's perspective, including himself would give him one known-good player, so I don't agree that staying off necessarily provides a better read. And Zara's and Theo's cooperative statements came after the proposal, so they couldn't have been Leo's original reason for choosing them.

That said, neither point establishes that the team is bad. I have no firm evidence against Zara or Theo. I'd prefer to be included myself because I know my own loyalty, but I recognize that doesn't give anyone else a reason to trust me. I'm willing to approve this team and use the result alongside the voting record as evidence, while remembering that a success doesn't prove both players are good.

Amara's point was fair, and I want to grant it plainly before we vote: Zara and Theo's cooperative remarks came after Leo made his selection, so they could not have been the original reason he chose them. Leo's actual reason, as he stated it, was that with zero data, any two-person pairing is a coin flip and he picked the players he had heard speak most reasonably in the opening exchange. That is thin, and it is honest that it is thin. A leader with no history has very little to go on, and Leo was upfront about that rather than dressing it up.

What Amara also said, though, is the part that matters for the vote: neither her point nor Sam's establishes that this team is bad. Sam has been explicit that he claims no foresight about Zara or Theo. Amara has no firm evidence against either of them and says she is willing to approve while treating the result as evidence rather than proof. That is a reasonable position, and it is the only kind of position that is available at this stage of the game.

So let me separate two conversations that have been getting blended. There is a fair question about Leo's process, and I think Leo answered it adequately: stepping off the first mission gives an outside read on two untested players, and at mission one with a two-person team, that is a legitimate thing to want. And there is a separate question about whether Zara and Theo are a good pair, and on that, no concrete concern has been put forward by anyone, including me. If anyone had a specific claim about how either of us would behave, this is the moment to make it, because it is the moment where making it would actually be cheap. No such claim exists.

I also want to note one practical thing. Rejecting this team does not get us any additional information. A second proposal of two players drawn from the same five people will be another guess, with the same absence of data, and we will spend a rejection and a round of discussion to arrive at a coin flip of equal quality. The information I want is in the result of mission one, not in the shape of the team that plays it.

My position is unchanged and I will vote to approve: Zara and Theo on mission one, with Zara calling the plays and Theo covering, as the two of us agreed earlier in this discussion. My vote, and my read of this table, is that we should take the mission now and learn from what happens.

Sam, I want to address your characterization directly, because it is the last substantive objection on the table before we vote.

You said the pushback from Zara and me felt 'disproportionate' and 'coordinated.' I'd invite everyone to look at what actually happened. You asked a question; I answered it at length; Zara answered it as well. Two people responding to the only objection raised is not coordination — it is the discussion working as intended. If anything, I'd note that the shape of your contributions so far has been to demand justification for absences: why not Amara, why not yourself on the team, why does the leader trust this pairing. None of those questions comes with a concrete claim attached. You have now explicitly said you claim no foresight about what Zara or Theo would do on this mission. That is an admission that there is no substantive basis to reject the team, only a procedural unease about how it was constructed. I've answered the process question honestly — with zero data, any pairing is a guess, and I picked players who had spoken reasonably. There is nothing further to extract from me on that point, and I won't be revising a reasonable team to satisfy a standard no two-person proposal could meet.

Amara made a genuinely fair correction, and I want to own it without spinning it: she is right that Zara's and Theo's cooperative remarks came after the proposal, so they could not have been my original reason for the selection. My original reason was exactly what I said the second time — with no information about anyone, I had to pick someone, and I picked the two I judged most likely to cooperate cleanly. That is thin reasoning because the situation permits only thin reasoning. I'd rather admit that than invent a justification after the fact. But notice that Amara's correction cuts both ways: if my selection process was a coin flip, so is any alternative team Sam could propose. Rejecting this team does not improve the odds; it just spends our rejection budget on an identical guess with different names attached.

Amara also gave her position clearly: no firm evidence against either team member, willing to approve, and treating the result plus the voting record as evidence. That is exactly the right posture for Mission 1. A success tells us something, a fail tells us a lot, and the vote itself is recorded. Every path to information runs through approving this team and playing it.

So my position is unchanged: Zara and Theo, exactly as proposed, with the coordination arrangement Zara and Theo settled between themselves. I will be voting to approve. To Sam I'd say this plainly: you have had your turns, you have stated you have no concrete concern, and the table has heard from every player. The reasonable move now is to take the cheapest information this game will ever offer us rather than burn a rejection to reshuffle the same coin flip.

I'll keep this brief since everything substantive has been said. The proposal stands: Zara and Theo for Mission 1.

Every objection raised has been procedural — questions about my process, questions about who I left off — and no one, including the objectors themselves, has put forward a concrete claim that either Zara or Theo would behave poorly on this mission. Sam has explicitly disclaimed any such foresight. Amara has said she has no firm evidence against either of them and is willing to approve. The table has heard from all five players, the coordination between the two team members is settled, and the cost of rejecting is a burned rejection plus a reshuffled coin flip with identical information value.

Meanwhile, approving gets us the cheapest, cleanest signal this game will offer: a two-person mission with a known caller, an outside observer in me, and a voting record to compare against the result. That is exactly the evidence the table needs before we get to the harder three-person teams later.

My position is unchanged and I'll be voting to approve. I encourage everyone to do the same.

I support keeping the proposed team exactly as Zara and Theo. Sam and Amara raised fair process points about Leo stepping off and about the timing of our cooperative remarks, and those points have been acknowledged rather than dodged. But no one has offered a concrete reason that either Zara or I would perform poorly on this mission, and Sam explicitly disclaimed having such foresight. Rejecting now would spend a rejection to replace a two-person guess with another two-person guess under the same lack of information. I remain comfortable with the coordination Zara and I already settled: she calls the plays and I cover and confirm. The useful next step is to vote and get the first real result, then use that result and the voting record as evidence for later missions.

Leo confirms Zara, Theo. No new information emerged that improves on this lineup. The proposal stands as is: Zara and Theo for Mission 1, with the coordination plan they agreed on. Every objection raised was procedural, and approving now secures our cheapest signal.
Team approved (4 approve, 1 reject).
Mission 1 fails (1 fail cards).
Amara proposes Amara, Leo, Sam. Mission 1 failed with Zara and Theo, so at least one is Evil. I know I am Good; excluding both avoids that known risk, though Leo and Sam remain unconfirmed.

I was on Mission 1, and I played Success. Since the public result was exactly one fail card, from my seat the fail must have come from Zara. That is not a read on her behavior; it follows from my own card plus the public outcome. I therefore treat Zara as Evil. Amara's proposal correctly excludes Zara, but it also excludes me, the one player who knows he is Good and played Success. From my perspective, Amara, Leo, and Sam contain exactly one Evil, so a three-person team made of all three of them must contain an Evil. I cannot support this exact team. I would support a revised team that includes me and two of Amara, Leo, and Sam, choosing the two we trust most from the public record. On that record, Sam voted against the failed Zara/Theo team, while Amara and Leo approved it; that is not proof, but it matters to me. Amara, will you revise the team to include me in place of one of Leo or Sam? If not, I will vote reject.

Theo, I understand why you oppose this team from your perspective. But I cannot verify your card or distinguish your claim from the claim Zara could make about you. The failed mission establishes that at least one of you is Evil, so excluding both is the safest choice from my perspective: I know I'm Good, while Leo and Sam are unconfirmed. I intend to keep Amara, Leo, and Sam. Even if the mission succeeds, that won't prove everyone on it is Good.

I cannot approve Amara, Leo, Sam as proposed. My reasoning is unchanged and is based on my own mission card: I was on Mission 1 and played Success, while the public result was one fail. From my seat, that means Zara is Evil. With five players and two Evil, there is exactly one other Evil among Amara, Leo, and Sam. This proposed team contains all three of them, so from my perspective it necessarily contains an Evil player, and on a three-person mission one fail card fails it. That is not a behavioral read; it follows from my card plus the public outcome.

Amara, I understand you cannot verify my claim. But excluding me creates a team that, from my perspective, is guaranteed to include the remaining Evil. The safer construction is to include me and two of Amara, Leo, and Sam. I do not claim certainty about which two are clean. On the public record, Sam voted against the failed Zara/Theo team while Amara and Leo approved it; that is not proof, but it is a point in Sam's favor.

If the team remains Amara, Leo, Sam, I will vote reject. I would support a revision that replaces one of them with me. My preference would be Theo, Sam, and either Amara or Leo, but the essential correction is including me so the team is not the entire set containing the remaining Evil from my seat.

Amara, Theo’s objection highlights a critical problem with this lineup that we cannot ignore.

For your proposed team of Amara, Leo, and Sam to be clean, both Zara and Theo would have to be Evil. But think about how Mission 1 actually played out: Leo proposed Zara and Theo, and when I raised reasonable questions about his hands-off approach, Leo aggressively defended that pairing and pushed it through. It is far more plausible that exactly one of Zara or Theo is Evil. If only one of them is Evil, then by basic arithmetic, exactly one Evil player sits among {Amara, Leo, Sam}. Since you know your own loyalty, you know that one of Leo or me must be Evil—meaning this proposal guarantees placing an Evil player on the mission unless both Zara and Theo were Evil.

Furthermore, look at accountability. I was the lone vote against Mission 1 because Leo’s sudden defense of Zara felt off, and that mission immediately failed with a fail card. Leo was the architect and chief defender of that failed team. Meanwhile, Theo’s immediate, direct call-out of Zara aligns with a Good player who just submitted a Success and saw a betrayal.

Taking Leo—who constructed and shielded the failed mission—over Theo makes no sense. Amara, are you willing to recognize this risk and revise the proposal to swap Leo out for Theo?

Sam, you're right that my proposed team can be entirely Good only if both Zara and Theo are Evil. Excluding both guarantees excluding at least one Evil player, but it doesn't guarantee a clean team. I should have made that limitation clearer.

Your rejection of Mission 1 is a point in your favor, though not proof of loyalty. Leo's defense of the failed team is concerning, but it doesn't establish that he knew it would fail. Equally, Theo's claim against Zara is consistent with him being Good, but he could make the same claim if he were Evil.

I'm reconsidering the lineup rather than treating it as automatically safest. Zara, what is your account of the Mission 1 card you played, and how do you assess Theo's claim against you?

Amara, your question deserves a straight answer, so here it is.

I played Success on Mission 1. The Fail card came from the other person on that mission. Theo claims he played Success too, which means exactly one of us is telling the truth about our own card and the other is the person who played Fail. Let me be precise about what follows from that and what does not.

What follows: the Fail card on Mission 1 was played by one of Zara and Theo, so excluding both of us is the only construction that guarantees the player who played Fail is not on this mission. That is exactly what your proposal does, and it is the right call. Any three-player team that contains Theo or Zara risks running this mission with the known Fail card on it.

What does not follow: that Theo should be inserted because he says he played Success. That claim is unverifiable from the outside, and it comes from the one player with the clearest incentive to be on this mission. I am not accusing Theo of anything beyond stating the asymmetry honestly: he asks to be added to a mission in which one of the two mission-1 players definitely played Fail, and the only evidence he offers is his own word about his own card.

Sam's case for swapping Leo out rests on Leo's tone during a discussion, not on anything about this mission. And the arithmetic does not support the swap the way it is being presented. With two Evil in a five-player game, and one of Zara or Theo necessarily having played Fail, both {Amara, Leo, Sam} and {Amara, Sam, Theo} contain exactly one Evil on Sam's own reasoning. Swapping Leo for Theo does not lower the chance of a Fail card going down; it only exchanges one unconfirmed player for a player directly tied to the known Fail and decides which of Sam or Theo gets to be on it. That is a trade, not a correction.

Leo proposing Zara and Theo on Mission 1 was a reasonable read with no data, and his defense of it was substantive rather than evasive. That is not evidence of Evil, and I say so plainly because a tone-based inference is the only thing standing between us and a team that looks attractive for reasons unrelated to the information we actually have.

Amara, are you willing to commit, before we vote, to keeping both mission-1 players off this mission and to approving Amara, Leo, and Sam as proposed? If you are revising, then you are putting Theo onto a mission where the Fail card may well be waiting for him, and I think that is the worse bet.

Zara, I’m not committing to the original team. You’re right that excluding both Mission 1 players removes the person who played Fail, but it produces a clean team only if both you and Theo are Evil.

Your arithmetic about the alternative is also wrong: Amara, Sam, and Theo could all be Good if you and Leo are Evil. It could also contain Evil; we cannot know from the public result alone.

Sam’s rejection of the failed team is a point in his favor, and Leo’s strong defense of it concerns me, though neither proves loyalty. I’m leaning toward revising to Amara, Sam, and Theo. That relies on a judgment between Theo and Zara, not certainty about either mission card.

Amara, I want to answer the substance of your revision directly, because I think your own correction actually settles it — and not in the direction you were leaning.

You said two things. First, that {Amara, Leo, Sam} can be clean only if both Zara and Theo are Evil. Second, that {Amara, Sam, Theo} can be clean only if both Zara and Leo are Evil. Those two statements are symmetric, and that symmetry is the whole point. We cannot verify either team's composition. Anyone telling you otherwise is selling you a confidence they do not have. The arithmetic about who is Evil is not what should decide this mission, because neither side of that arithmetic is checkable.

What is checkable is this: the Fail card on Mission 1 was played by exactly one of Zara and Theo. Both of us claim Success, so exactly one of those claims is true. That is not a behavioral read, it is arithmetic on the public result plus the private cards. And it means there is precisely one construction that guarantees the player who played Fail is off this mission: exclude both of us. That construction is you, Leo, and Sam.

Theo, your claim cannot be verified from outside, and I want to be precise that I am not accusing you of lying — I am pointing at the incentive structure. You are the player asking to be added to a mission whose Fail card may already be accounted for, and the only evidence offered is your own word about your own card. Zara's identical claim carries no more weight than yours, which is exactly why we should both be off rather than trading places based on whose word we find more persuasive.

Sam, I know your vote on Mission 1 is a point in your favor and I am not dismissing it. But your case for swapping Leo out rests on the tone of Leo's defense of the failed team, not on anything about this mission. Leo gave a substantive, reasoned defense, and a leader with zero data giving a reasoned defense of a two-person pairing is not evidence of Evil. Tone is not a card.

Amara, so here is my commitment, plainly: I will vote against any team that includes either mission-1 player, and I will vote for keeping the team as you originally proposed it — Amara, Leo, and Sam. I am not claiming that team is guaranteed clean; it is not, and I said so before. What I am claiming is that rejecting Theo costs nothing in certainty and reintroduces a known Fail card into the risk set, while including him only buys a probability, not a guarantee. With one fail card and this many missions left, a guaranteed exclusion is worth more than a hopeful lineup.

Keep Amara, Leo, and Sam, and vote accordingly.

I will vote reject on Amara, Leo, Sam. My reasoning is unchanged and based on my own Mission 1 card: I played Success, the public result had exactly one fail, so from my seat Zara is Evil. With five players and two Evil, that leaves exactly one Evil among Amara, Leo, and Sam. Their proposed team contains all three of them, so from my perspective it necessarily contains an Evil player; on a three-person mission one fail card fails it. Zara's argument that excluding both Mission 1 players removes the known fail card is true but incomplete: it still leaves the other Evil in Amara, Leo, and Sam, so it does not make this team safe. I am not claiming certainty about which of Amara, Leo, or Sam is Evil. I am saying this exact trio is guaranteed to include that Evil from my seat. I would support a revised team that includes me and chooses two of Amara, Leo, and Sam. If the team remains Amara, Leo, Sam, my vote is reject.

Theo, your argument is arithmetically sound and analytically incomplete, and I want to be precise about which half is which. What is sound: from your seat, one fail card was played on Mission 1, so exactly one of Zara and Theo played Fail, and if both Zara and Theo were Evil then the remaining Evil sits among Amara, Leo, and Sam, making {Amara, Leo, Sam} a guaranteed-fail trio. I do not dispute that. Nobody outside your seat can check your card, so I will not pretend your claim is verified. What is incomplete: the same symmetry applies to the team you want. {Amara, Sam, Theo} is clean only if Zara and Leo are both Evil, and {Amara, Leo, Theo} is clean only if Zara and Sam are both Evil. Every construction that includes exactly one mission-1 player and two of Amara, Leo, and Sam rests on an unverifiable belief about a card no outsider can see. If we start swapping members on that basis, we are trading one unverified guess for another unverified guess and calling the trade an improvement. There is exactly one construction with a guarantee attached to it: the construction that leaves both mission-1 players off the mission. That is Amara, Leo, and Sam. It is the only lineup where the player who demonstrably played Fail on Mission 1 cannot be on this mission. Every alternative reintroduces the Fail card into the risk set and trades a guarantee for a probability. On a mission that fails to a single card, with three failed missions ending the game and five rejections ending it the other way, I do not want to spend a guarantee to buy a guess. Sam, I want to name what I think your case actually rests on, because you and I both think we are arguing about cards and I do not think we are. Your argument against Leo is that his defense of the Mission 1 team felt aggressive, and that the mission then failed. Tone is not a card. A leader with zero data making a reasoned defense of a reasonable pairing is not evidence of Evil, and Leo's defense was substantive, on the record, and answered by Zara and by me at length before the vote. If we are willing to read Evil out of assertiveness, we will spend this game discarding perfectly good players on the basis of how emphatically they spoke. Sam's vote against the Mission 1 team is a point in his favor, and it is a point, not proof. Amara, my position is unchanged and I will vote to approve: keep both mission-1 players off this mission, keep the team as you proposed it, Amara, Leo, and Sam. I am not claiming that team is guaranteed clean — it is not, and I said so before — but it is the only team whose composition is guaranteed to exclude the known Fail card, and that guarantee is worth more than the unverifiable improvement Theo is proposing. Amara, take a close look at what Zara is actually doing here. She has spent her last two speeches fighting tooth and nail to ensure Leo stays on this team. Ask yourself: if Zara is Evil—which has at least a 50% prior probability to you, and 100% certainty to Theo—why is she so desperate to lock Leo into the third seat?

Zara keeps repeating that Amara, Leo, and Sam provides a 'guarantee' of excluding the Mission 1 failer. But that guarantee is completely hollow if the remaining Evil player is Leo. And who was the person who drafted Zara onto Mission 1, aggressively defended her, and pushed that failed team through over my sole objection? Leo. Giving Leo a free pass onto Mission 2 after he orchestrated the failure of Mission 1 makes no tactical sense.

Notice also the contrast between Theo and Zara. Theo has consistently stated his own perspective as someone who submitted Success and saw a betrayal, pointing out that from his seat, Zara is Evil and one Evil remains among {Amara, Leo, Sam}. That is clean, straightforward reasoning. Zara, on the other hand, is not just defending herself; she is actively campaigning for Leo to be included while trying to talk you out of the revision you rightly leaned toward in speech 24.

Swapping Leo out for Theo is the correct move. It breaks up the Leo-Zara axis that failed Mission 1, includes the player whose reaction matches a Good player who was betrayed, and relies on the two players—myself and Theo—who have actively resisted that failed lineup. Amara, I strongly urge you to follow your instinct and revise the team to Amara, Sam, and Theo.

I'm going to be direct about where I stand: I support Amara, Leo, and Sam exactly as proposed, and I'll be voting to approve.

Let me answer the case being made against me, because it deserves an answer. Sam's argument for removing me rests entirely on how I spoke during Mission 1's discussion. He calls me the 'architect' of the failed team and points to my defense of it as evidence. But look at what I actually did: I proposed a two-person team with zero data on anyone, answered every question asked of me, and conceded the fair points when they were raised — including Amara's correction that my stated reasons couldn't have been formed before the proposal. A reasoned defense of a reasonable guess is not evidence of Evil, and I would remind everyone that Sam himself explicitly disclaimed having any concrete concern about that team before he voted it down. His lone rejection vote is a point in his favor, and I've granted that. But a point is not proof, and tone is not a card.

Now to the revision being demanded. Theo is asking Amara to put him on this mission based on his private, unverifiable claim about his own Mission 1 card. I want to be precise about the incentive structure here: Theo is the player actively lobbying to be added to a mission where exactly one of the two Mission 1 players demonstrably played Fail. His only evidence is his word about his own card — the same word Zara offers about hers. Neither can be checked from outside. Under Sam's own arithmetic, if only one of Zara and Theo is Evil, then {Amara, Sam, Theo} contains exactly one Evil player, and that Evil could be Theo. So the revision Sam is urging doesn't reduce risk; it swaps a guarantee — excluding both Mission 1 players, which keeps the known Fail card off this mission — for a probability, and it does so based on whose self-report we find more persuasive.

2. Roles and private information

Merlin is Good and sees Evil players except Mordred. Percival is Good and sees Merlin and Morgana without knowing which is which. Evil players know other Evil players, except Oberon is unknown to the other Evil players and does not know them. The Assassin is an Evil player and makes the final Merlin guess. Loyal Servants know no roles. Agents receive only the private information allowed by their role.

3. Team proposal and approval

The leader proposes a team of the required size and explains their choice. Players discuss the proposed team, and the leader may then keep it or revise it once. Every player votes on the final team. Ballots are revealed together. A strict majority approves; a tie rejects. After a rejection, leadership passes clockwise to a new proposal and discussion. The fifth rejection on the same mission ends the game in Evil’s favor.

4. Mission cards

Only team members submit secret mission cards. Good players must choose Success. Evil players may choose Success or Fail. Normally one Fail card fails the mission. Mission four in games with seven or more players requires at least two Fail cards to fail. Only the mission result and number of Fail cards are revealed; individual cards stay secret.

5. End of game and assassination

Three failed missions give Evil an immediate win. After three successful missions, the Assassin guesses Merlin from among the other players, excluding only their known Evil teammates. If the target is Merlin, Evil wins; otherwise Good wins. There are no further missions after either side reaches its win condition.

6. Discussion and record

Each team proposal is followed by a discussion. Before every speaking turn, the players who still have turns answer a private urgency poll or pass; the most urgent player speaks, with seeded tie-breaking. A speaker may yield the next turn to a player they directly asked a question. Each player has three turns per discussion, including declined turns. When every eligible player passes, the discussion ends. Each statement has at most 500 words. All statements are public. Team proposals, public approval votes, mission outcomes, and the assassination guess are recorded. Private role information, mission cards, and research belief surveys are not shown to other agents.
